W1-1.note: Every 'help' (broken basin, rags in the drawer, hidden dust, cutting lace) does harm the narrator never notices.

W1-2.note: Papa says she makes the very best use of her time now; growing up to be a help is mamma's line.

W1-3.note: 'Muss after Maria' and 'a big pile of dust she left' while she went to the door imply Maria had swept it up to clear later; E (overlooked) is the narrator's framing and arguable.

W1-4.note: She plans to cut the lace off mamma's best suit, a final 'help' the reader sees will ruin it.

W1-5.note: A 'waist' of a walking suit with sleeves is a bodice or blouse.

W1-6.note: She says Bessie 'only plays while there's work going on' and isn't 'so much use as I am'.

W2-1.note: The passage centers on her hurt at Father's veto and Mother explaining it is necessity, not lack of sympathy.

W2-2.note: $11.25 among fifteen girls is seventy-five cents apiece.

W2-3.note: Musing whether Mother ever wishes for things she doesn't get suggests Mother quietly does without.

W2-4.note: A presentation address is a formal speech.

W2-5.note: 'If he would only soften it a little... A blunt no is a great deal harder to bear.'

W2-6.note: Contrasting rich Florence with girls who must think twice about a dollar sets up why the plan is hard for some.

W3-1.note: The violet calms them by pointing to scent and renewal that copies lack; A is a partial misreading of the fading lines.

W3-2.note: 'Worked in colored worsted' means embroidered in wool.

W3-3.note: 'Oh, don't joke on such a subject' and the disapproving 'No' show they thought it too serious for jest.

W3-4.note: She wishes the bee had been fooled because it would serve him right, 'the thief'.

W3-5.note: The hubbub is the fuss the violet later calls foolish and without real cause.

W3-6.note: The violet asks whether hidden blossoms will replace dead ones in copies, implying they cannot.

W4-1.note: The passage argues the 'bookworm' is really over thirty common pest species masquerading under a misnomer.

W4-2.note: He failed to recognize his two 'species' as larva and imago of one.

W4-3.note: People meet these pests daily with no unusual interest while still wondering what a bookworm is.

W4-4.note: A 'curious and interesting characterization' is a strange, peculiar one.

W4-5.note: The author wryly jokes about defective ear drums and a different kind of cock in Mentzel's day.

W4-6.note: The question is cited as a reaction against the fantastical accounts, i.e., doubt.

W5-1.note: The central discovery is that the 'flowers' are flesh-eating animals.

W5-2.note: She admires the complete illusion created by light from above.

W5-3.note: The theater with the stage 'all around' conveys lit tanks surrounding the visitor in dark aisles.

W5-4.note: Using a flower term for the hidden body shows she still frames them as flowers; D is arguable but she says she couldn't tell whether it had a body.

W5-5.note: The keeper's 'charges' are those in his care, i.e., wards.

W5-6.note: The meat, a tiny ball of dry pulp, slowly sank to the bottom.

W6-1.note: All sources on freeze-thaw trace to Lindquist's single unpublished dissertation.

W6-2.note: Sediments from mountain streams built up in layers in the lake; it was shallow, not 200 miles deep.

W6-3.note: The three works the website cites all credit freeze-thaw to Lindquist.

W6-4.note: Greatest concentration of hoodoos means densest cluster.

W6-5.note: She calls warming a 'grave threat' and worries we cannot adapt without the science.

W6-6.note: She contrasts the figurative 'reshaping' of attitudes with the park literally being reshaped.
